1. Koka, a word occurring in the Rigveda^1 and the Atharva-
veda,^2 seems to denote the ‘cuckoo.’ In all the three passages
in which it is found, Sāyaṇa explains it as the Cakravāka.
Roth^3 renders it in the Atharvaveda passages as a certain
destructive parasitic animal. Cf.

) vii. 104, 22 (koka-yātu, a ghost in
the shape of a cuckoo).
2) v. 23, 4; viii. 6, 2.
3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, s.v., 6.
Cf. Bloomfield, Hymns of the Athar-
vaveda, 454; Whitney, Translation of
the Atharvaveda, 262; Geldner, Rig-
veda, Glossar, 49; Zimmer, Altindisches
Leben, 92.

2. Koka is mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (xiii. 5,
4, 17) as a son of the Pañcāla king, Sātrāsāha.

Kokila, a very frequent word in the Epic and later, denoting
the cuckoo, is only inferred for the Vedic period from its being
the name of a Rājaputra in the Kāṭhaka Anukramaṇī.^1
1) Weber, Indische Studien, 3, 460.
